Watchmen
wŏch´men
n. pl. (sentries on the wall; rendering Hebrew tsaphah and shamar)
From watch, to keep awake. The watchman's whole office is wakefulness on behalf of sleepers.

Biblical Definition

Watchmen stand on the wall to warn. Ezekiel makes the office a picture of the prophet, with the blood-guilt spelled out: “if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned… his blood will I require at the watchman's hand” (Eze 33:6). Isaiah rebukes watchmen who are blind, ignorant, and “loving to slumber” (Isa 56:10), and sets others on Jerusalem's walls who “shall never hold their peace day nor night” (Isa 62:6). The psalmist adds the limit of all watching: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain (Psa 127:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a watchman as a sentinel; a guard; one set to watch, especially in the night, for the security of a city or camp.

expand to see more

WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one set to watch in the night.

2. One whose business is to guard against danger, and give notice of it.

Key Scripture

Eze 33:6 — "But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand."

Isa 56:10 — "His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber."

Isa 62:6 — "I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence,"

Psa 127:1 — "A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain."

Modern Corruption

The watchman's office has been claimed by the perpetually alarmed, who blow the trumpet at everything, and abandoned by the comfortable, who blow it at nothing.

expand to see more

Ezekiel 33 sets terms that make the office serious in both directions. If the watchman warns and the people ignore him, he has delivered his soul; if he sees the sword and stays silent, the blood is required at his hand. The trumpet is not for the watchman's satisfaction but for the city's survival, which means a man who enjoys sounding it has misunderstood the job as thoroughly as the man who sleeps through it.

Isaiah 56:10 diagnoses the failure with unusual bite: his watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark. The image is of a guard dog that will not make noise — harmless, well-fed, and useless. Psalm 127:1 then keeps the whole office humble: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain. The wall is watched by men; it is kept by God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsaphah (H6822), to look out, keep watch; shamar (H8104), to guard; shomer, a keeper — the same root as Cain's question about his brother.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsaphah (H6822) — to watch, look out; Ezekiel 3:17 and 33:2-7, I have set thee a watchman.

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard; Psalm 127:1, Song 3:3, the watchmen that go about the city.

Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to be watchful; Mark 13:37, what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.

Usage

"“His blood will I require at the watchman's hand” — silence has a price."

"“Dumb dogs, they cannot bark” — the harmless, useless guard."

"“Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” — the limit of all vigilance."
